# Evidence dossier: Yoga

*Evidence dossier 590 — Yoga. Every exhibit catalogued, every ruling stated with its grounds.*

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Yoga
- **Original script:** योग
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Convention:** IAST — macrons for long vowels, underdots for retroflexes, the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 590 of 597

## The Evidence

**Exhibit 1 — the attestation.** The attested form is **योग**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Yoga**.

**Exhibit 2 — the flattened form.** The plain form *yoga* differs from the canonical **Yoga** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

**Exhibit 3 — the physical record.** The discipline leaves postures, not temples: the Mohenjo-daro seal of a figure in yogic seat (its identity debated), the Mathura images of śramaṇa ascetics, and the modern globe’s studios. The oldest ‘monument’ is the human body arranged to be still.

**Exhibit 4 — the continuing record.** Some two hundred million people practise asana today — the largest following of any discipline in the lexicon.  ‘Yoga’ entered English as a loan-word a century ago and now needs no italics.

## The Convention's Own History

Long before IAST was formalized in 1912, Sanskrit had Pāṇini — the fourth-century-BCE grammarian whose rules describe the language's sounds with a precision no other ancient tradition matched. That heritage is why the convention is so exact: retroflexes (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ) are not accented dentals but separate phonemes with separate meanings; long and short vowels (ā/a, ī/i, ū/u) change words, not just timing. IAST writes those distinctions down with underdots and macrons so that a reader who has never heard Sanskrit can still read it *correctly*. Dropping the marks is not transliteration at a lower resolution — it is a different, lesser claim.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Yoga** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

## The Verdict

Case closed on **Yoga**: canonical, cited, and defended. The keyboard form *yoga* is the same name in another register of display — always acceptable. The register's files remain open: if a source surfaces that changes any line of this entry, the entry changes. Until then, the temple at [/yoga/](/yoga/) holds the canonical form.

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3 (the chariot simile), Bhagavadgītā 2.48 (yoga as skill in action), Patañjali, Yoga-sūtra 1.2 and 2.29.
